Hp.definition: ISA altitude corresponding to the local static pressure. Positive: pressure below ISA sea-level pressure.
Hp.limits: Pressure-altitude model: −5 to 84.852 km geopotential. Geometric altitude is converted before the atmosphere calculation.
Hp.physics: Hydrostatic balance relates pressure to altitude in the layered ISA atmosphere. Inverting that pressure profile gives an equivalent pressure altitude, not a measurement of height above the ground.

Hg.definition: Geometric height above mean sea level. Positive: above mean sea level.
Hg.limits: Pressure-altitude model: −5 to 84.852 km geopotential. Geometric altitude is converted before the atmosphere calculation.
Hg.physics: Geometric height measures distance above sea level. The spherical-Earth conversion accounts for weakening gravity when converting between geometric and geopotential altitude.

P.definition: Absolute static pressure of the surrounding air, related to density and absolute temperature by the ideal gas law.
P.limits: Pressure-altitude model: −5 to 84.852 km geopotential. Geometric altitude is converted before the atmosphere calculation.
P.physics: The ISA hydrostatic pressure profile represents the weight of the air column above the selected level. Local density then follows the ideal-gas relation using the entered temperature.

Δ ISA.definition: Difference between actual static air temperature and ISA temperature at the same pressure altitude. Positive: warmer than ISA.
Δ ISA.physics: The temperature offset changes the local thermal state at the same pressure altitude. Warmer air at fixed pressure has lower density; colder air has higher density.

OAT.definition: Static temperature of the surrounding air.
OAT.physics: Static air temperature sets density and sound speed. Adding the ISA temperature offset gives the local temperature without changing the selected pressure level.

TAS.definition: Magnitude of aircraft velocity relative to the surrounding air. Nonnegative.
TAS.physics: True airspeed measures motion through the air mass. Combining it with local density sets dynamic pressure; combining it with local sound speed gives Mach number.

CAS.definition: Airspeed at ISA sea-level conditions producing the same impact pressure as the actual flight condition. Nonnegative.
CAS.physics: The subsonic isentropic Pitot relation converts actual impact pressure to the speed that gives the same impact pressure at ISA sea level; compressibility is included.

EAS.definition: Airspeed at ISA sea-level conditions producing the same dynamic pressure as the actual flight condition. Nonnegative.
EAS.physics: Equivalent airspeed preserves dynamic pressure: q = 0.5 ρ TAS² = 0.5 ρ₀ EAS². Unlike CAS, it is not defined by impact pressure.

Mach.definition: Ratio of true airspeed to local speed of sound. Nonnegative.
Mach.limits: 0 ≤ M < 1 for the current compressibility model.
Mach.physics: Mach compares airspeed with the speed of pressure disturbances in the local air. The pitot conversion used here describes subsonic, isentropic deceleration with gamma = 1.4.

CL.definition: Aerodynamic lift divided by the product of dynamic pressure and wing reference area. Positive: lift toward the aircraft upper side.
CL.physics: The lift equation balances aerodynamic lift against the selected normal load, n times weight. Increasing mass or load factor requires more dynamic pressure or a larger lift coefficient.

Vs Factor.definition: Input multiplier applied to reference 1-g stall speed in CAS, with an optional additive CAS increment. Nonnegative multiplier.
Vs Factor.physics: The input factor scales the 1-g stall speed expressed as CAS; the optional additive increment is specified in knots. It does not change the reference stall speed or model accelerated stall.

Ground Speed.definition: Magnitude of aircraft horizontal velocity relative to the ground. Nonnegative.

Qdyn.definition: Kinetic energy per unit volume of the air-relative flow. Nonnegative.
Qdyn.physics: Dynamic pressure is kinetic energy per unit volume of moving air. It scales aerodynamic forces and rises with density and the square of true airspeed.

Qc.definition: Difference between stagnation pressure and static pressure. Nonnegative in the adopted subsonic model.
Qc.physics: A pitot opening brings the flow to rest and converts kinetic energy into compression. Impact pressure is stagnation minus static pressure; it approaches dynamic pressure at low Mach number.

Weight.definition: Aircraft weight, expressed as mass in the selected units for aerodynamic calculations. Nonnegative.
Weight.physics: Although traditionally labeled weight, this input is a mass-equivalent value in kg (or other mass units). Gravitational weight force is W = m g₀.

Sref.definition: Wing reference area used to define aerodynamic coefficients. Positive area.
Sref.physics: Reference area is the chosen normalization area in the lift equation. A larger area produces more lift at the same dynamic pressure and lift coefficient; it does not determine wing shape.

cref.definition: Wing reference chord used to calculate Reynolds number. Positive length.
cref.physics: Reference chord sets the length scale for Reynolds number. Comparing inertial transport with molecular viscosity at that scale characterizes the flow regime; this calculation does not predict transition or separation.

CLmax.definition: Maximum lift coefficient attainable at the onset of stall for the selected aircraft configuration. Positive coefficient.
CLmax.physics: The limiting lift coefficient sets the lowest 1-g speed that can support the aircraft weight. Its value must come from aircraft data for the chosen flap configuration; the calculator does not predict it from geometry.

NzPullup.definition: Ratio of aerodynamic lift to aircraft weight in an unbanked maneuver. Positive: lift toward the aircraft upper side.
NzPullup.physics: Normal load factor is lift divided by weight. The unbanked pull-up model increases lift demand without introducing the bank relation used for a level turn.

NzTurn.definition: Load factor in a coordinated level turn. Positive and not less than 1 in the adopted model.
NzTurn.physics: In a coordinated level turn, the vertical component of lift balances weight and the horizontal component provides centripetal acceleration. This gives n = 1/cos(bank), with bank magnitude below 90 degrees.

BankTurn.definition: Aircraft bank angle in a coordinated level turn. Positive: right wing down.
BankTurn.physics: In a coordinated level turn, the vertical component of lift balances weight and the horizontal component provides centripetal acceleration. This gives n = 1/cos(bank), with bank magnitude below 90 degrees.

Track.definition: Direction of the aircraft horizontal ground-velocity vector, measured clockwise from true north. Positive: clockwise (ground-velocity vector to the right).

Heading.definition: Direction in which the aircraft nose points, measured clockwise from true north. Positive: clockwise (nose to the right).

Sideslip.definition: Angle between the aircraft longitudinal axis and the incoming relative wind. Positive: relative wind coming from the right.

Drift.definition: Angular difference between heading and ground track (heading minus track). Positive: heading to the right of track.

HeadWind.definition: Wind component along the selected runway/reference direction. Positive: wind from ahead. Negative: tailwind.

Wind Speed.definition: Magnitude of horizontal wind velocity. Nonnegative.

CrossWind.definition: Wind component perpendicular to the selected runway/reference direction. Positive: wind coming from the right. Negative: wind from the left.

Runway Angle.definition: Direction of the selected runway/reference axis, measured clockwise from true north. Positive: clockwise (reference direction to the right).

Wind Direction.definition: Direction from which the wind blows, measured clockwise from true north. Positive: clockwise (wind-from direction to the right).

mass.MTOW.definition: Maximum takeoff weight approved for the aircraft, expressed as mass in the selected units.
mass.MTOW.use: Reference mass for takeoff-condition calculations when selected.
mass.MTOW.physics: The conventional aircraft-data name uses weight, while the profile stores the numerical mass equivalent used by the calculator.

mass.MLW.definition: Maximum landing weight approved for the aircraft, expressed as mass in the selected units.
mass.MLW.use: Reference mass for landing-condition calculations when selected.
mass.MLW.physics: The conventional aircraft-data name uses weight, while the profile stores the numerical mass equivalent used by the calculator.

mass.MZFW.definition: Maximum zero-fuel weight, excluding usable fuel, expressed as mass in the selected units.
mass.MZFW.use: Reference mass for zero-fuel-mass calculations when selected.
mass.MZFW.physics: The conventional aircraft-data name uses weight, while the profile stores the numerical mass equivalent used by the calculator.

mass.BOW.definition: Basic Operating Weight as defined by the aircraft manufacturer.
mass.BOW.use: Stored reference mass for calculations that use the selected aircraft mass.

mass.Heavy.definition: User-defined heavy reference weight, expressed as mass in the selected units.
mass.Heavy.use: User-defined reference mass for calculations that use the selected aircraft mass.
mass.Heavy.physics: Heavy is a user-defined loading reference, not a regulatory weight limit.

mass.Light.definition: User-defined light reference weight, expressed as mass in the selected units.
mass.Light.use: User-defined reference mass for calculations that use the selected aircraft mass.
mass.Light.physics: Light is a user-defined loading reference, not a regulatory weight limit.

CLmaxFlap.full: Maximum lift coefficient by flap setting
CLmaxFlap.definition: Maximum lift coefficient for the specified flap configuration. Positive coefficient.
CLmaxFlap.use: Used with mass, density, and reference area to calculate reference stall speed.
CLmaxFlap.physics: The limiting lift coefficient sets the lowest 1-g speed that can support the aircraft weight. Its value must come from aircraft data for the chosen flap configuration; the calculator does not predict it from geometry.

Pressure Altitude.definition: ISA altitude corresponding to the local static pressure. Positive: pressure below ISA sea-level pressure.
Pressure Altitude.limits: Pressure-altitude model: −5 to 84.852 km geopotential. See the documented geometric-altitude temperature convention.
Pressure Altitude.physics: Hydrostatic balance relates pressure to altitude in the layered ISA atmosphere. Inverting that pressure profile gives an equivalent pressure altitude, not a measurement of height above the ground.

Geometric Altitude.definition: Geometric height above mean sea level. Positive: above mean sea level.
Geometric Altitude.limits: Pressure-altitude model: −5 to 84.852 km geopotential. See the documented geometric-altitude temperature convention.
Geometric Altitude.physics: Geometric height measures distance above sea level. The spherical-Earth conversion accounts for weakening gravity when converting between geometric and geopotential altitude.

Pressure.definition: Absolute static pressure of the surrounding air, related to density and absolute temperature by the ideal gas law.
Pressure.physics: The ISA hydrostatic pressure profile represents the weight of the air column above the selected level. Local density then follows the ideal-gas relation using the entered temperature.

Temperature.definition: Static temperature of the surrounding air.
Temperature.physics: Static air temperature sets density and sound speed. Adding the ISA temperature offset gives the local temperature without changing the selected pressure level.

Delta ISA.definition: Difference between actual static air temperature and ISA temperature at the same pressure altitude. Positive: warmer than ISA.
Delta ISA.physics: The temperature offset changes the local thermal state at the same pressure altitude. Warmer air at fixed pressure has lower density; colder air has higher density.

True Airspeed.definition: Magnitude of aircraft velocity relative to the surrounding air. Nonnegative.
True Airspeed.physics: True airspeed measures motion through the air mass. Combining it with local density sets dynamic pressure; combining it with local sound speed gives Mach number.

Calibrated Airspeed.definition: Airspeed at ISA sea-level conditions producing the same impact pressure as the actual flight condition. Nonnegative.
Calibrated Airspeed.physics: The subsonic isentropic Pitot relation converts actual impact pressure to the speed that gives the same impact pressure at ISA sea level; compressibility is included.

Equivalent Airspeed.definition: Airspeed at ISA sea-level conditions producing the same dynamic pressure as the actual flight condition. Nonnegative.
Equivalent Airspeed.physics: Equivalent airspeed preserves dynamic pressure: q = 0.5 ρ TAS² = 0.5 ρ₀ EAS². Unlike CAS, it is not defined by impact pressure.

Lift Coefficient CL.definition: Aerodynamic lift divided by the product of dynamic pressure and wing reference area. Positive: lift toward the aircraft upper side.
Lift Coefficient CL.limits: Available when dynamic pressure and reference area are positive. The sign follows the selected load factor.
Lift Coefficient CL.physics: The lift equation balances aerodynamic lift against the selected normal load, n times weight. Increasing mass or load factor requires more dynamic pressure or a larger lift coefficient.

Dynamic Pressure.definition: Kinetic energy per unit volume of the air-relative flow. Nonnegative.
Dynamic Pressure.physics: Dynamic pressure is kinetic energy per unit volume of moving air. It scales aerodynamic forces and rises with density and the square of true airspeed.

Impact Pressure.definition: Difference between stagnation pressure and static pressure. Nonnegative in the adopted subsonic model.
Impact Pressure.physics: A pitot opening brings the flow to rest and converts kinetic energy into compression. Impact pressure is stagnation minus static pressure; it approaches dynamic pressure at low Mach number.

Bank Angle φ.definition: Aircraft bank angle in a coordinated level turn. Positive: right wing down.
Bank Angle φ.physics: In a coordinated level turn, the vertical component of lift balances weight and the horizontal component provides centripetal acceleration. This gives n = 1/cos(bank), with bank magnitude below 90 degrees.

Track Angle.definition: Direction of the aircraft horizontal ground-velocity vector, measured clockwise from true north. Positive: clockwise (ground-velocity vector to the right).

Heading Angle Ψ.definition: Direction in which the aircraft nose points, measured clockwise from true north. Positive: clockwise (nose to the right).

Drift Angle.definition: Angular difference between heading and ground track (heading minus track). Positive: heading to the right of track.

Sideslip Angle β.definition: Angle between the aircraft longitudinal axis and the incoming relative wind. Positive: relative wind coming from the right.

Ground Speed.definition: Magnitude of aircraft horizontal velocity relative to the ground. Nonnegative.

Vs Factor.definition: Ratio of current calibrated airspeed to reference 1-g stall speed in CAS. Nonnegative.
Vs Factor.physics: This dimensionless output is current CAS divided by the 1-g reference stall CAS. It is not an accelerated-stall speed or a maneuver load factor.

Mach.definition: Ratio of true airspeed to local speed of sound. Nonnegative.
Mach.limits: 0 ≤ M < 1 for the current compressibility model.
Mach.physics: Mach compares airspeed with the speed of pressure disturbances in the local air. The pitot conversion used here describes subsonic, isentropic deceleration with gamma = 1.4.

Wind Speed.definition: Magnitude of horizontal wind velocity. Nonnegative.

Wind Direction.definition: Direction from which the wind blows, measured clockwise from true north. Positive: clockwise (wind-from direction to the right).

Geopotential Altitude.definition: Altitude equivalent to gravitational potential energy per unit mass under constant standard gravity. Positive: above the reference datum.
Geopotential Altitude.equation: H = r h / (r + h); for Hp/P input, H = Hp − 29.271247 ΔT ln(p/p0)
Geopotential Altitude.limits: Pressure-altitude model: −5 to 84.852 km geopotential. See the documented geometric-altitude temperature convention.
Geopotential Altitude.physics: Geopotential height represents gravitational potential using standard gravity. When derived from pressure altitude, the calculator applies its specified temperature-offset model; this is not simply geometric height.

Density Altitude.definition: ISA altitude corresponding to the actual air density. Positive: above ISA sea level.
Density Altitude.physics: Density altitude is the ISA level with the same air density as the current condition. It summarizes density effects on aerodynamic forces without claiming that the aircraft is physically at that height.

Temperature Altitude.definition: Tropospheric ISA altitude corresponding to actual static temperature, limited to 11 km in this model. Positive: above ISA sea level.
Temperature Altitude.physics: The calculation uses the tropospheric ISA lapse rate and caps temperatures at or below 216.65 K at 11 km. Temperature alone cannot identify a unique altitude across all ISA layers.

Density.definition: Mass of air per unit volume, calculated from static pressure and absolute temperature using the ideal gas law. Positive scalar.
Density.physics: The ideal-gas equation links density to static pressure and absolute temperature for dry air. At the same pressure, heating expands the air and reduces its mass per unit volume.

Total Temperature.definition: Stagnation temperature obtained by adiabatically bringing the air-relative flow to rest.
Total Temperature.physics: Adiabatic deceleration converts kinetic energy into internal energy, raising temperature as the air is brought to rest. The ideal stagnation relation uses a constant specific-heat ratio of 1.4, without a probe recovery correction.

Viscosity.definition: Dynamic viscosity of air relates shear stress to velocity gradient; its temperature dependence is modeled by Sutherland's law. Positive scalar.
Viscosity.physics: Air viscosity represents molecular momentum transport. Sutherland's law models its dependence on static temperature: dynamic viscosity increases with temperature and sets the viscous scale in Reynolds number.

Sound Speed.definition: Speed of propagation of small pressure disturbances in the surrounding air. Positive scalar.
Sound Speed.physics: Small pressure disturbances propagate through ideal air at a speed set by absolute temperature and the specific-heat ratio. Warmer air has a higher sound speed.

Stall Speed Vs.definition: Reference 1-g calibrated airspeed at which the required lift coefficient equals CLmax for the selected aircraft mass and configuration. Nonnegative.
Stall Speed Vs.equation: Vs,TAS = √(2 m g0 / (ρ S CLmax)); displayed Vs,CAS = CAS(Vs,TAS)
Stall Speed Vs.physics: At the 1-g stall reference, maximum lift just balances weight. The result is converted from TAS to CAS; maneuver load factor does not alter this reference value.

Reynolds.definition: Ratio of inertial to viscous effects based on true airspeed and reference chord. Nonnegative.
Reynolds.physics: Reynolds number compares inertial and viscous effects over the reference chord. Increasing speed, density, or chord increases this ratio; increasing viscosity reduces it.

Pressure Ratio δ.definition: Ratio of local static pressure to standard sea-level pressure. Positive scalar.
Pressure Ratio δ.physics: Dividing static pressure by standard sea-level pressure gives a dimensionless atmospheric pressure scale. It is used to normalize weight and compare conditions across pressure levels.

Density Ratio σ.definition: Ratio of local air density to standard sea-level density. Positive scalar.
Density Ratio σ.physics: The density ratio compares local air density with standard sea-level density. Its square root relates true and equivalent airspeed at equal dynamic pressure.

Temperature Ratio θ.definition: Ratio of local absolute temperature to standard sea-level absolute temperature. Positive scalar.
Temperature Ratio θ.physics: The temperature ratio compares absolute local temperature with the standard sea-level temperature. Absolute temperature is required because molecular thermal energy sets sound speed and the ideal-gas density relation.

Total Pressure.definition: Stagnation pressure of the air-relative flow under isentropic conditions.
Total Pressure.physics: Stagnation pressure is the pressure after ideal subsonic, isentropic deceleration to rest. Adding pitot impact pressure to static pressure gives this total pressure; shocks and flow losses are not modeled.

DynPressure * S / g.definition: Aerodynamic reference force qS expressed numerically in kilogram-force (kgf). Nonnegative.
DynPressure * S / g.physics: Dynamic pressure times reference area gives an aerodynamic force scale before multiplying by a force coefficient. Dividing by standard gravity expresses that force in kgf; it is not aircraft mass.

Lift Force.definition: Aerodynamic lift force required by the selected load factor. Positive: lift toward the aircraft upper side.
Lift Force.equation: L / g0 = q S CL / g0 (displayed as kgf)
Lift Force.physics: Lift is dynamic pressure times reference area and lift coefficient, and equals the selected normal load times weight. The displayed kgf value converts that force using standard gravity.

Weight/Delta W/δ.definition: Aircraft weight divided by atmospheric pressure ratio δ. Positive for positive aircraft weight.
Weight/Delta W/δ.physics: Dividing weight by pressure ratio normalizes the aircraft load to standard sea-level pressure. The kgf display is a force normalization, not a change in the actual aircraft mass.

Load Factor Nz.definition: Ratio of aerodynamic lift to aircraft weight. Positive: lift toward the aircraft upper side.
Load Factor Nz.physics: Normal load factor measures lift relative to weight. In the level-turn mode it follows the vertical lift balance; in pull-up mode it is supplied directly.

Turn Radius.definition: Signed radius of a coordinated level turn relative to the air mass. Positive: right turn. Negative: left turn.
Turn Radius.physics: The radius and turn rate use true airspeed in a coordinated level-turn model. A steady wind translates the air-relative circular path; the ground path is not generally circular.

Turn Rate.definition: Rate of change of aircraft heading in a coordinated level turn. Positive: clockwise (right turn).
Turn Rate.physics: The rate is calculated for a coordinated, constant-altitude turn using true airspeed and bank angle. The sign follows turn direction, not wind direction.

AlongTrack Headwind.definition: Wind component along the aircraft ground track. Positive: wind from ahead. Negative: tailwind.

AlongTrack Crosswind.definition: Wind component perpendicular to the aircraft ground track. Positive: wind coming from the right. Negative: wind from the left.
